title: The Randomized-Transformer Control
takeaway: On the paper's automated activation score, features found in a random-weight transformer get a slightly higher median than the real features do. Splitting the randomized features on whether they are "single token" shows where that advantage comes from: the single-token half is trivially easy to score, and on everything else the real features win while the randomized ones sit about where polysemantic neurons sit. The panel is the paper's own warning that a good automated interpretability score, taken alone, is not evidence that a decomposition found real structure.
walkthrough:
Two populations of features are compared, score by score. Magenta is run A/1, the [[dictionary-learning]] run whose [[feature]] set the paper studies throughout. Yellow is the same autoencoder procedure applied to a [[randomized-transformer]] — a copy of the one-layer model whose weight matrices have had their entries shuffled in place, so the weight distributions are preserved and only the learned structure is destroyed ([[weight-shuffling]]).

Where the two histograms overlap, the bars render dark orange. The small triangles below each axis mark each group's median, per the legend at top right.

### The three scores in the top row

Left is [[automated-interpretability]] on activations: Claude writes an explanation of a feature, then uses only that explanation to predict activations on unseen text, and the score is the [[spearman-correlation]] between predicted and true. Middle is the same explanation used to judge unseen high-logit tokens, scored as accuracy against a half-real, half-random mix, so $0.5$ is chance ([[automated-logit-scoring]]). Right is a blinded annotator's [[feature-interpretability-rubric]] score.

Two of the three go the way the paper expects. The randomized model's logit accuracy piles up on chance, which is unsurprising given its output weights are shuffled. On the rubric, magenta sits higher.

The left panel does not. Its banner says so: "Randomized Seems Better??"

### The inset

The inset splits that awkward panel in two, on one binary property. A feature counts as single token if, across all twenty examples in its top [[activation-interval]], the same token carries the largest activation ([[single-token-features]]).

On the left half, the randomized features dominate, with a tall spike of near-perfect scores. Predicting "fires on this one token" is easy to explain and easy to score.

On the right half the ordering reverses, and the paper notes the randomized curve there resembles the distribution for [[polysemanticity|polysemantic]] neurons.

So the randomized model's apparent win is composition, not quality ([[randomized-feature-bimodality]]). It learns more, and more strictly, single-token features — which the paper reads as dictionary learning picking up regularities of the dataset rather than of the model ([[model-vs-data-question]]) — and those inflate its median on a score that rewards easy explanations.

terms.definition: The magenta population: features from dictionary learning run A/1, the run trained on the real (trained) one-layer transformer that supplies nearly all the paper's examples. Here it is the reference group the control is measured against.

The yellow population: features from running the same sparse autoencoder on MLP activations of a one-layer model whose weights were randomly shuffled. It is an ablation asking how much feature structure survives when the model has learned nothing.

Used interchangeably in this figure for the same control. The randomization shuffles the entries within each weight matrix of the trained model rather than drawing fresh random values, so each matrix keeps its distribution of weights and loses only its structure.
The legend at top right explains that each small triangle under an axis marks the median of the same-colored distribution. Medians are the summary the appendix's comparisons are stated in.
The left top panel. It scores how well Claude, given only its own written explanation of a feature, can predict that feature's activations on text it has not seen.

The score for that panel: correlation of predicted and true activations computed on ranks rather than raw values. It runs from -0.4 to 1.0 here, with 1.0 meaning the predicted ordering of activations matches the true one exactly.

The histograms in the two automated panels and both insets are normalized to integrate to one within each group. This lets the magenta and yellow populations be compared even though they contain different numbers of features.
The manual panel plots raw counts instead of density, because human scoring produced only a few hundred scored intervals in total.
The yellow banner over the left top panel, flagging that on this one score the control group has the higher median. The question marks signal that the authors do not take the result at face value.
The middle top panel. Using the same generated explanation, Claude is asked whether an unseen token with a high output logit is one this feature should promote.
Fraction of those binary logit judgments that are correct, scored against a 50/50 mix of genuine top-logit tokens and random tokens. Chance is therefore 0.5.
The magenta banner appearing over the middle and right top panels and over the right inset, marking the comparisons where the real features come out ahead.

The right top panel. A blinded human annotator (one of the authors) formed an interpretation of each feature and scored it, sampling examples across the full activation spectrum rather than only the top ones.

The annotator's total score on the paper's five-part rubric: confidence in the interpretation, consistency of high activations with it, consistency of the positive logit effects, effect-size separation, and specificity.
Not a third group. Where the magenta and yellow histograms cover the same bin, the bars are drawn over each other and read as dark orange.
A reference line on the correlation axes marking zero correlation — the score assigned when Claude's prediction carries no information about the true activations.

The narrow yellow column sitting on the zero line in the left panel and, larger, in the right inset. When Claude predicts a constant value — usually all zeros — no correlation can be computed and the paper assigns a score of zero, which stacks features at that one point.

The subset of features whose top activation interval is dominated by one and the same token in every example. The paper calls this behavior trivial, because an explanation of such a feature is just the name of a token.
The complementary subset: features whose strongest activations do not always land on the same token. This is where the paper says the interesting comparison lives.
The yellow banner over the left inset, stating that on single-token features the randomized model's features score higher.
The same Spearman activation score as the left top panel, redrawn on each half of the split. The insets sum to that panel, which is what the "+" between them denotes.
A reminder that the two inset populations are a partition of the left top panel's yellow and magenta distributions, not two new experiments.

One of eleven evenly spaced bands between zero and a feature's maximum activation. Both the human and automated evaluations draw examples from across all of them, so that a feature is judged on weak activations as well as its top ones.

Ordinary MLP neurons that fire for several unrelated things at once; they are the paper's baseline for uninterpretable. The appendix says the not-single-token randomized features have a score distribution close to theirs.
The shape claimed for the yellow population: two separated clumps rather than one spread. The inset shows the clumps are the single-token and non-single-token groups.

numbers.meaning: Range of the Spearman correlation axis in the left top panel and both insets. It stops well short of -1 because predictions that are actively anti-correlated with the truth are rare.

Medians in the left top panel, read off the triangles: magenta (A/1) at roughly 0.57, yellow (randomized) at roughly 0.62. The yellow triangle sitting to the right of the magenta one is the entire anomaly the figure exists to explain.
Height of the yellow spike sitting on zero correlation in the left top panel. It is the accumulation of features for which Claude gave a constant prediction, which the paper scores as zero.
Height of the yellow peak near correlation 0.9-1.0 in the left top panel — the pile of near-perfectly-scored randomized features that the inset attributes to single-token behavior.
Range of the accuracy axis in the middle top panel, since accuracy on a binary judgment is a fraction of correct answers.

Chance accuracy in the middle panel, because the tokens shown are a 50/50 mix of genuine top-logit tokens and random ones. The yellow median sits exactly here, which the appendix calls unsurprising: the randomized model's output weights carry no learned structure for an explanation to predict.
Height of the yellow density spike at accuracy 0.5 in the middle panel. Randomized features cluster tightly on chance rather than spreading around it.
Median logit accuracy for A/1 features, stated in the main text and matching the magenta triangle at about 0.75. The comparison values are 0.53 for neurons and 0.5 for the randomized transformer.
Range of the manual rubric axis. The maximum is 14 rather than 15 because a perfect score on the effect-size-separation item (worth 1) implies the specificity item is not applicable.

The five component ranges of the rubric that sum to the Rubric Value: confidence in the interpretation, consistency of high-activation tokens, consistency of positive logit effects, whether inconsistent logit effects were separated by effect size, and specificity.

Medians in the manual panel: yellow (randomized) at about 7, magenta (A/1) at about 12. The main text gives 12 as the median scored feature interval, meaning a confident, specific hypothesis consistent with the logit weights.

The tall yellow bar at zero in the manual panel: randomized features the annotator could not form any hypothesis about. Zero is also the median score the annotator gave polysemantic neurons in the main text, which is why the appendix reads this bar as one mode of a bimodal distribution.
The tallest magenta bars in the manual panel, at the top of the scale. Most A/1 feature intervals land near the rubric maximum.
Number of examples in a feature's top activation interval. A feature is labeled single token only if the largest activation falls on the same token in all twenty.

Medians in the left inset (single-token features): magenta about 0.65, yellow about 0.83. The gap is the paper's evidence that the randomized model's single-token features are not merely more numerous but more strictly single-token, firing on the same token even in weak intervals, which makes them easier to score.
Height of the yellow peak just below correlation 1.0 in the left inset — the high-scoring peak the appendix points to as trivially earned.
Medians in the right inset (not single token): yellow about 0.18, magenta about 0.39. Here the ordering reverses, and the randomized distribution is said to resemble that of polysemantic neurons.
Height of the yellow zero-correlation spike in the right inset. Constant, uninformative explanations are concentrated in the non-single-token randomized features.
Per feature, Claude predicts activations for 60 dataset examples of nine tokens each, giving 540 predictions from which the Spearman correlation on the left panel is computed.
Number of evenly spaced activation intervals between zero and a feature's maximum activation, used by both the human and automated evaluations so that weak activations are tested too.
Total activation intervals scored (412) across features and neurons (162) in the manual analysis. The small sample is why the right top panel plots counts rather than density.

For the logit score, Claude judges 100 tokens per feature: 50 random ones and the 10th through 60th largest positive logits. The top 10 are withheld because they were used to generate the explanation.
